fatal_errors: The proposed standalone friction stir processing repair does not reconstruct the SPS-consolidated high-entropy-alloy electrode and electrospark-deposition coating intervention.
The cited evidence supports FSP primarily as a pre-weld treatment followed by fusion welding, not as a standalone method for restoring an already damaged region or replacing missing material.
The hypothesis asserts validation under aggressive high-temperature service conditions, whereas the target study performed no corrosion, wear, geothermal-environment, or service-performance testing.
The assumed nickel-based superalloy and its liquid-film hot-cracking mechanism do not match the mechanically alloyed CrFeNiMo-family powders and C1018 steel substrate.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad theme of avoiding fusion-welding hot cracking and offers a testable alternative, but it diverges from the target in material system, processing route, parameters, structural mediators, baselines, and measured outcomes. The target used temperature-dependent SPS to produce machinable HEA electrodes, followed by three- or six-layer electrospark deposition on C1018 steel. Its central tradeoff was improved compact densification at higher SPS temperature and better coating coverage—but greater roughness, oxidation, pores, and microfissures—with six ESD layers. The proposed experiment has a clear comparator and falsification rule, but FSP and fusion welding may not constitute equivalent repairs because standalone FSP does not necessarily replenish damaged material. Evidence E1 and E2 establishes that FSP can refine microstructure and reduce cracking during subsequent fusion welding, but it does not substantiate the claimed standalone repair or aggressive-service performance.
